explanations: terra: The worshiper's declaration “You alone we serve” supplies the عبد side of the path requested in the following ayah.
terra: The request for guidance to the straight path follows worship in 1:5, explicitly meeting the section's servant and trodden-road senses.
terra: God makes earth a bed and sky a built canopy, placing level ground and unsupported divine architecture together.
terra: A struck rock releases twelve springs by God's command, setting divine opening of stone beside Thamud's painstaking apertures.

luna: The section describes raised structures and mountains later leveled. This ayah recalls a mountain raised above the Israelites when they took a covenant, a divine height held over people rather than built for human permanence.

luna: The section defines صَخْر as large, hard stone and pairs it with Thamud’s rejection of messengers. This ayah compares hardened hearts to stone, then says some stones split or fall in awe of God—a stone-centered counterimage to rejection. | terra: Stones split and release water or fall in awe of God while some hearts are harder, showing hard rock opened and lowered without human carving.

luna: The section makes human elevation answerable to God’s command. This ayah again places the mountain above the Israelites with the covenant and tells them to hold firmly to what was given, a repeated scene of imposed height and obligation.
terra: God is the unprecedented originator of heavens and earth, relocating true production without a prior model from a celebrated city to divine creation.
terra: Abraham and Ishmael raise the House's foundations while asking God to accept their work, contrasting prayerful construction with architecture meant to immortalize its makers.
terra: God constricts and expands and to Him people return, placing material limitation and abundance within return rather than personal worth.
terra: A town lies fallen upon its roofs before God demonstrates restoration, putting ruined construction and renewed creation in the same episode.
terra: Abraham asks to see revival so his heart may become reassured, connecting inward tranquility to witnessed re-creation after disassembly.

luna: The section links hard rock with works whose trace is erased. This ayah pictures a smooth stone with a thin covering left bare by rain, a specific image of exposed stone and vanished covering, though its own subject is failed charity.

luna: The section questions the claim that reduced provision means God has humiliated someone and shows rulers’ height ending. This prayer says God gives and removes sovereignty and honors or abases whom He wills, placing worldly rank under His authority. | terra: God grants and removes dominion, exalts and abases, placing every human rise and fall under the same agency.
terra: Jesus says to worship God and calls that the straight path, explicitly pairing service with a road.
terra: Divine aid is made good news so hearts may become reassured, locating tranquility in trust rather than monuments or provision.
terra: Death reaches people even inside lofty fortified towers, directly denying that height and strong building can secure permanence.

luna: The section describes mountains and structures whose height cannot last. This ayah recalls the mountain raised over the people for their covenant, another formulation in which a mountain’s position marks a boundary set by God.
terra: Earlier generations were more firmly established, supplied with rain and rivers, yet destroyed for their sins, another material-strength reversal.

luna: The section’s named خ ل ق branch means bringing something forth without a prior model. This ayah calls God the Originator of the heavens and earth and says He created all things, placing Iram’s claimed novelty beside a Creator’s making. | terra: God is again named the originator of heavens and earth, marking the boundary between created marvels and the One who initiates creation.

luna: The section contrasts ground flattened by force with a road made smooth by being walked, then calls the soul into God’s servants. This ayah says to follow God’s straight path and not diverging paths, making the chosen route a concrete moral counterpart.
terra: Hud reminds Aad that God increased them in bodily stature, joining their exceptional height and strength to gifted creation rather than self-made greatness.
terra: After Hud's warning, Aad's last remnant is cut off, reinforcing the section's secondary image of a once-visible trace erased.

luna: The section’s Semud image is people cutting houses into rock. Salih’s speech here says they carved homes from mountains and built palaces in the plain, joining mountain-work to settlement. | terra: Salih recalls Thamud building palaces on plains and carving mountains into houses, the fullest parallel to the valley's rock-cut architecture.

luna: The section pairs Thamud’s impressive works with an account of human height and lowliness. This ayah contrasts the arrogant chiefs with those regarded as weak, showing status division among the same people who carved the mountain homes.

luna: The section presents Thamud’s construction alongside their transgression. This ayah says the arrogant ones rejected what Salih’s followers believed, making the community’s haughtiness explicit before the camel incident in 7:77.
luna: The section gives Thamud’s rock-built security and their prostrate end. This preceding ayah supplies their defiance and killing of the she-camel; 7:78 gives the collapse that follows.

luna: The section says Thamud ended prostrate in their dwelling places after cutting secure homes from rock. This ayah places them in their homes, brought low after their rebellion; the built refuge has become the setting of their collapse. | terra: The rock-carving Thamud end جاثمين in their own homes, brought from confident construction to bodies collapsed against the ground.

luna: The section describes Pharaoh’s tower and stakes among human works that cannot endure. This ayah says God destroyed what Pharaoh and his people made and erected, giving the physical reversal of that architecture. | terra: God destroys what Pharaoh and his people manufactured and what they had raised, directly extending the ruler's fall to his constructions.

luna: The section defines د ك ك as breaking a wall or mountain until it is level with the earth. In Moses’ encounter, the mountain is made dakk and Moses falls unconscious, a direct mountain-crushing scene. | terra: At the divine disclosure the mountain is made دكا and Moses falls unconscious, directly enacting the section's named root as height becomes level ground.

luna: The section contrasts the apparent security of rock-built homes with mountains brought low. This ayah depicts a mountain held above a people like a canopy as they fear its fall, making the same material a threat rather than shelter.
terra: The same reassurance formula makes victory only a means for hearts to rest, while help itself remains from God.
terra: Wealth and children are explicitly called a trial, clarifying why abundance in surah 89 cannot by itself mean honor.
terra: A building founded on a crumbling brink collapses with its builder, making moral foundation and structural fall one exact image.
terra: Those satisfied and مطمئن with the nearer life locate their rest in the passing ground, the opposite orientation from return to God.
terra: Pharaoh is described as high in the land and one of the extravagant, explicitly coupling elevation with exceeding bounds.

luna: The section’s dictionary memory calls Iram a desert marker and presents Pharaoh as a ruler who sought to rise toward heaven. This ayah says Pharaoh’s body was preserved as a sign for later people, making the fallen ruler a marker after his failed rebellion.

luna: The section pairs Thamud’s carved settlement with their end in their dwellings. This parallel account says the cry seized the wrongdoers and left them prostrate in their homes; 11:68 then says it was as if they had never lived there. | terra: The blast seizes Thamud and they lie جاثمين in their dwellings, repeating the fall from secure rock houses to immobility.

luna: The section’s Thamud houses are followed by people brought low in their home. This neighboring account says it was as if they had never lived there, connecting collapse to the erased trace named by the section’s dictionary branch. | terra: Thamud appear as though they had never flourished in those dwellings, directly realizing the section's image of a vanished built trace.

luna: The section’s م ث ل discussion holds a standing form and a form leveled to earth in one word. This account of earlier towns says some are still standing and some have been cut down, giving that opposed posture as a history of settlements. | terra: The histories of towns include some still standing and others reaped flat, an unusually exact Quranic pairing of upright trace and leveled remnant.

luna: The section relates cities’ destruction to the peoples’ overreach. This neighboring ayah says the towns were not wronged but wronged themselves, completing 11:100’s standing and cut-down settlements with the cause of their fall.

luna: The section says Iram’s raised columns need physical support and that human height fails when its column falls. This ayah says Allah raised the heavens without columns visible to people, shifting the same vertical image from dependent construction to divine power. | terra: The heavens are raised بغير عمد ترونها, using the section's عماد root while contrasting divine elevation with human height that needs visible supports.
terra: God spreads earth and places firm mountains in it, another creation formula pairing horizontal habitation with stable height.
terra: God expands and constrains provision while worldly life is only brief enjoyment, placing material plenty and restriction within one larger scale.

luna: The section’s dictionary branch for مُطْمَئِنَّة carries a low, settled contour. This ayah uses the same root for hearts finding rest in God’s remembrance; treating inner rest as the image’s low ground is an uncertain extension. | terra: Hearts find طمأنينة in God's remembrance, clarifying the inward rest named by the section's tranquil soul beyond its physical low-ground sense.
terra: The good word is a tree with firm root and branch in heaven, offering a vertical form whose lasting height depends on a sound foundation.
terra: The corrupt word is like a tree uprooted from the earth with no stability, an organic version of height collapsing when its support is lost.
terra: People dwell in the homes of former wrongdoers after their fate has become clear, turning ruined habitation into a visible warning.

luna: The section describes the present earth and mountains losing their distinct heights at judgment. This ayah says the earth will be changed for another earth and the heavens as all come before God, another specific formulation of that transformed scene. | terra: The earth is replaced by another earth when all emerge before God, enlarging the section's leveled judgment ground beyond altered topography.
terra: Earth is spread and firm mountains cast upon it, repeating the divine arrangement that judgment later dismantles.
terra: Every thing is held in divine stores and sent down only in known measure, a precise parallel to making and provisioning by proportion.

luna: The section’s dictionary branch for ع ب د calls a well-used road a smoothed, trodden way and reads the invitation among God’s servants beside it. This ayah names a straight path to God, making the path-and-servant association explicit. | terra: A straight path is named immediately before the protected “My servants” of 15:42, making the section's service-and-road meeting textual.

luna: The section connects entry among God’s servants with a trodden-road image. This next ayah names God’s servants and says Satan has no authority over them except followers who go astray, completing the straight-path statement in 15:41. | terra: “My servants” have no satanic authority over them on the straight path named in 15:41, joining destination, service and way.

luna: The section calls Hicr the home of Thamud and says its people denied the messengers. This ayah identifies the people of al-Hijr as rejecters of messengers, grounding the rock-dwelling scene in its own context. | terra: This ayah names the people of al-Hijr and their rejection of messengers, fixing the حجر place-name and moral identity for the carving scene in 15:82.

luna: The section pairs the people of Hicr’s rejection of messengers with their confidence in rock-carved homes. This intervening ayah says they were given signs but turned away, showing that their material security accompanied refusal of guidance.

luna: The section describes Thamud cutting homes into the hardest rock and says they felt secure there. This ayah gives the exact mountain-carved, secure-house scene. | terra: The people of Hijr carve houses from mountains while feeling secure, exactly matching the section's delicate opening of massive hard rock.

luna: The section says the secure rock dwellings did not protect Thamud from an end arriving in the morning. This neighboring ayah names the cry that seized them at morning; 15:82 supplies the houses, while this row supplies their sudden end. | terra: The blast catches the secure mountain-carvers in the morning, showing how abruptly the confidence of 15:82 fails.

luna: The section says the mountain-cut houses felt secure but could not save their makers. This ayah immediately adds that what they had earned did not avail them, making the failure of security explicit. | terra: What Thamud had acquired avails them nothing after 15:82-83, denying saving power to their skilled rock architecture.
terra: The Prophet is told to lower his wing to believers, another chosen lowering set against tyrannical self-elevation.

luna: The section sets human stakes against supports God places in the world and recalls Iram as a desert marker. This ayah describes mountains set firm, roads, and guidance, a related scene of fixed orientation without naming marker stones. | terra: God casts firm mountains into earth lest it sway and makes rivers and roads, explaining what divine earth-pegs do rather than merely how they look.

luna: The section’s labeled memory for Iram is a stone set as a landmark in open country. This ayah names landmarks and star-guidance, supporting the wayfinding function though it does not say the landmarks are stones. | terra: God provides landmarks and stars for guidance, contrasting useful orientation with Aad's playful markers on every height.
terra: The question “is one who creates like one who does not create?” places خلق and likeness-comparison together while drawing the creator-created boundary.
terra: God comes at a building from its foundations and its roof falls upon its makers, precisely showing that when support fails the height above it goes too.
terra: Every community is told to worship God and avoid الطاغوت, directly opposing عبد to the same root-field of transgressive height.

luna: The section’s dictionary branch for ع م د includes a tent pole. This ayah describes portable skin shelters alongside homes; it supplies a Qur’anic tent scene for that secondary sense, although it says nothing about poles. | terra: God gives portable dwellings from animal hides, a Quranic tent scene that sets the section's tent-pole sense beside marble permanence.
terra: A heart can remain مطمئن in faith under outward coercion, separating inward tranquility from status, safety or visible ease.
terra: A secure, مطمئنة town with abundant provision turns to hunger and fear through ingratitude, uniting city, tranquility, provision and reversal.
terra: A town's affluent people rebel and it is utterly destroyed, joining material elevation, boundary-breaking and civilizational collapse.
terra: The believer is told to lower the wing of humility to parents, offering a deliberate bodily metaphor for gentle descent.
terra: God expands provision for some and constrains it for others with full knowledge, separating measured رزق from personal worth.

luna: The section treats rising beyond a limit as arrogance. This ayah forbids arrogant walking and says a person cannot split the earth or reach the mountains in height, making the boundary of human ascent concrete. | terra: The proud walker can neither split the earth nor reach the mountains in height, fixing a concrete limit on human vertical ambition.
terra: The challenge to become stone or iron if one doubts resurrection turns maximum hardness into no barrier to God's recreating power.
terra: God says He has honored all children of Adam, locating human dignity in divine gift rather than abundance, height or monumental power.
terra: The Creator of heavens and earth is able to create the like of human beings, placing خلق and مثل together against any finite claim to be unmatched.

luna: The section describes mountains and human works losing their height. This neighboring judgment scene removes the mountains, leaves the earth exposed, and gathers everyone; 18:48 then places them in a row. | terra: Mountains are removed, the earth is left bare and all people are gathered, staging the open judgment ground after vertical landmarks vanish.

luna: The section’s 89:22 image has the Lord arrive with angels in ranks on the flattened ground. Here people are presented to their Lord in a row after the mountains have been removed in 18:47, joining leveling to ordered assembly. | terra: Humanity is presented before the Lord صفا on the bare ground of 18:47, matching the section's row-like plain and judgment rows.
terra: A wall about to collapse is restored, a literal scene of failing structure repaired for a merciful purpose hidden beneath it.

luna: The section cites Dhul-Qarnayn’s barrier as a built work that God will eventually flatten. This preceding ayah introduces the barrier between the mountains and Dhul-Qarnayn’s offer to build it with the people’s help. | terra: Dhul-Qarnayn asks for blocks of iron and fills the gap between two heights, beginning the massive barrier later made دكاء.

luna: The section says even a formidable wall has a divinely set end. This ayah details the iron and molten-copper construction of Dhul-Qarnayn’s barrier; 18:97 then says the people could neither climb nor pierce it. | terra: Iron is heated and covered with molten copper, specifying the formidable material construction whose promised leveling gives 18:98 its force.

luna: The section contrasts tall structures with the earth made level at God’s appointed time. This ayah says Gog and Magog cannot climb or pierce the completed barrier, making its present strength specific before 18:98 names its eventual leveling. | terra: The barrier cannot be scaled or pierced, establishing its apparent impregnability immediately before God promises to level it.

luna: The section says even a built height will be flattened when God’s promise arrives. Dhul-Qarnayn says his barrier is a mercy for now and that his Lord will make it level when the promise comes, a constructed defense with a divinely set end. | terra: Dhul-Qarnayn says that when God's promise comes, even the formidable barrier will be made دكاء, so constructed security lasts only by divine leave.
terra: Jesus again names worship of the one Lord as a straight path, repeating the meeting between عبد and traversable way.
terra: The heavens nearly rupture, earth splits and mountains collapse, another sequence in which the greatest structures cannot bear a false divine claim.
terra: Whole generations disappear until neither a person nor even a whisper is sensed, closely matching the section's erased-trace detail.

luna: The section’s dictionary branch for ط غ ي treats transgression as rising beyond a limit and applies it to Pharaoh. This ayah gives Moses the command to confront Pharaoh because he has transgressed, a repeated formulation in Pharaoh’s story. | terra: Moses is sent to Pharaoh because he طغى, directly naming the ruler's act as crossing the limit.

luna: The section names Pharaoh among those who cross their bounds. Here Moses and Aaron are jointly sent to Pharaoh for the same stated reason, repeating the transgression that motivates the mission. | terra: Moses and Aaron are jointly sent to Pharaoh with the repeated diagnosis إنه طغى.

luna: The section contrasts the flattened earth with the road made traversable through use. In Moses’ exchange with Pharaoh, this ayah says God made the earth a resting place and its paths for travel, grounding the path image in God’s creation. | terra: God makes earth a cradle and threads roads through it, a direct nonlexical parallel to the section's ground made fit for passage.
terra: Pharaoh's magicians are told to come in a single صف, a human display-row that will shortly collapse into their voluntary prostration.

luna: The section cites the answer that mountains become a level plain. This preceding ayah asks about the mountains and introduces the response in 20:106–107; its contribution is the question that frames their removal. | terra: The question about the mountains introduces the explicit answer in 20:106-107 that their place will be a perfectly level plain.

luna: The section cites the land left as a level plain after the mountains are removed. This ayah gives that flat expanse, tying the section’s dekk image to the mountain-removal scene. | terra: After 20:105 asks about the mountains, this ayah says God leaves their place a level قاعا صفصفا, the very flat-field image developed in the section.

luna: The section cites a surface with neither hollow nor rise. This ayah specifies no crookedness or elevation on the plain, so the distinction between standing heights and low ground disappears. | terra: The plain of 20:106 has neither crookedness nor rise, specifying what remains when every separate height has disappeared.

luna: The section distinguishes ground smashed flat from a path made smooth by walking and speaks of entering among God’s servants. This next ayah says people follow the caller without deviation and voices are humbled, linking the level plain to a directed, humbled response.
terra: Faces are humbled before the Living Sustainer and the bearer of wrongdoing fails, staging universal human lowering on the judgment ground.
terra: Many wrongdoing towns are shattered and replaced by other peoples, a direct city-scale counterpart to breaking a wall or mountain.
terra: The shattered people of 21:11 are made like reaped growth and extinguished, specifying their movement from standing life to flattened residue.

luna: The section treats pegs as supports that steady what is above them. This ayah says firm mountains were placed in the earth so it would not shake and mentions passes as roads, assigning stability and passage to God’s world. | terra: Firm mountains and broad passes are placed on earth so people may be guided, combining anchoring heights with traversable ground.
terra: The sky is made a protected roof, another divine form of shelter whose security does not depend on a visible human column.
terra: No human before Muhammad was granted immortality, placing an explicit boundary against building as though one could remain forever.
terra: Every soul dies and is tested with both adversity and good before returning, supplying the governing frame for the two material trials in surah 89.
terra: Abraham questions his people's devotion to تماثيل, carrying the section's likeness root into standing fashioned representations.
terra: Abraham reduces the statues of 21:52 to fragments, a small-scale enactment of erected human forms being broken down.
terra: God teaches David the craft of armor for human protection, treating skilled manufacture as taught service rather than autonomous greatness.
terra: A person is مطمئن only while worldly good lasts and turns away under trial, distinguishing circumstantial ease from the section's truly tranquil soul.

luna: The section moves from raised structures to forced lowering and says no human height persists. This ayah places the sun, moon, stars, mountains, trees, creatures, and many people in prostration, then says the one God humiliates has no one to honor him. | terra: Creation including mountains bows to God, and one whom God يهن has no one to honor him; chosen prostration and imposed abasement meet here.
terra: Ruined towns lie collapsed upon their roofs beside an abandoned well and a lofty palace, gathering built height and its desolation in one landscape.
terra: God holds the sky from falling upon earth except by permission, another direct counterimage to loads borne by human columns.
terra: Successive bodily formation culminates in “another creation” and praise of the best of creators, moving the craft vocabulary into living form.
terra: Pharaoh and his chiefs act arrogantly toward Moses and Aaron and are called a lofty people, another formulation of height as rebellion.
terra: The question whether wealth and sons are being hurried to people as benefits exposes the same mistaken reading of material increase as favor.
terra: The answer to 23:55 is that they do not perceive, explicitly rejecting prosperity as a transparent measure of divine honor.
terra: The section's carving definition uses a garment's جيب as its model aperture; this ayah names those garment openings in an actual clothing scene.
terra: God permits certain houses to be raised so His name is remembered in them, giving elevated building a worshipful purpose opposite Aad's playful monuments.

luna: The section’s craft reading of خ ل ق includes measuring material before cutting. This ayah pairs creation with precise determination, giving a related measure-and-making formulation, though its root is not the source’s craft verb. | terra: God creates everything and determines it with exact measure, joining خلق to تقدير just as the section's craft definition joins making to measuring before cutting.
terra: Past peoples are each given explanatory examples and then utterly destroyed, joining مثل as lesson to the fate of human powers.

luna: The section contrasts being forced low with the chosen lowliness of a gentle walk and explicitly cites this root use. Here the servants of the Merciful walk on earth humbly, a positive, voluntary counterpart to fallen monuments. | terra: The servants of the Merciful walk the earth هونا, making voluntary gentleness and lowliness the answer to tyrants who force themselves upward.

luna: The section reads Iram’s height and its dictionary memory of Iram as a desert marker together. Hud’s question about placing a sign on every high place for play gives that raised-marker image a specific Qur’anic scene. | terra: Hud asks Aad why they build a sign on every height in play, directly staging Iram's passion for erecting conspicuous markers.

luna: The section says Ad’s structures look as though their builders expect to live forever. Hud’s next question names their constructed works and that very presumption of lasting life. | terra: Aad take monumental structures as though they might remain forever, making explicit the permanence fantasy carried by the section's tall buildings.

luna: The section groups Ad’s high-place monuments with transgression. In Hud’s same speech, this ayah says they seize others like tyrants, giving their architectural overreach a concrete form of domination. | terra: Immediately after Aad's monuments, Hud condemns their tyrannical striking, showing that the architecture belongs to a broader posture of coercive power.

luna: The section moves from Ad’s constructions and claim to lasting power toward their disappearance. This concluding ayah in Hud’s account says they denied him and were destroyed, supplying the fate after 26:128–130. | terra: Aad's destruction follows the monument and strength speech of 26:128-130, completing that passage's rise-and-fall arc.

luna: The section emphasizes the skill and force needed to open hard rock. Salih’s warning here names their skillful carving of houses from mountains, a direct formulation of that craft. | terra: Thamud carve houses from mountains with confident skill, foregrounding the same union of precise craft and hard material.
terra: The punishment seizes Thamud after their mountain carving in 26:149, supplying that version of the craft's failed security.
terra: The command to lower one's wing to believing followers repeats humility as a deliberate posture.

luna: The section’s ج و ب dictionary example measures rock-cut openings by a garment’s neck opening. In Moses’ sign before Pharaoh, this ayah puts his hand into the garment opening, repeating the aperture detail in a second account. | terra: Moses is told to put his hand into his جيب before confronting Pharaoh, placing the section's collar-opening image inside the Pharaoh cycle.

luna: The section’s distinctive mountain settlement ends as a place without its people. This ayah points to Thamud’s houses left empty because of their wrongdoing, joining the carved dwellings to the trace of a vanished community. | terra: Thamud's houses stand desolate because of their wrongdoing, a direct Quranic view of the built city after its builders are gone.

luna: The section treats mountains and stone structures as heights that can be brought down. This ayah says mountains that appear fixed will pass like clouds on the Day of Judgment, overturning the appearance of permanence. | terra: Mountains that appear fixed pass like clouds, exposing the apparent solidity of even the greatest natural structures as provisional.

luna: The section says transgression is going above a boundary and names Pharaoh’s overreach. This ayah says Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and divided its people, giving that upward domination its political form. | terra: Pharaoh exalts himself in the land, making moral overreach spatial through علا في الأرض exactly as the section explains upward transgression.

luna: The section’s dictionary branch for ج و ب compares cutting a hard-rock opening to making a garment’s neck opening. In Moses’ encounter with Pharaoh, this ayah puts his hand into his garment opening, supplying the soft-material aperture used by the section’s comparison. | terra: The command to insert the hand into the جيب is repeated in the very surah that also contains Pharaoh's tower, connecting two details developed by the section.

luna: The section describes Pharaoh ordering mud fired and a tower made so he can ascend toward Moses’ God. This ayah stages that precise construction and intention in Pharaoh’s own command. | terra: Pharaoh orders Haman to fire clay and build a tower so that he may look toward Moses' God, the section's other human bid for height.
terra: Pharaoh and his forces act arrogantly in the land and suppose they will not return, joining elevation to the illusion of permanence.
terra: God seizes Pharaoh and his forces and casts them into the sea, the downward answer to the arrogance of 28:39 and tower of 28:38.

luna: The section takes Iram as a singular city whose makers could not preserve its height. This ayah recalls many destroyed prosperous towns whose dwellings were not inhabited after them, making abandoned architecture the remainder of worldly power. | terra: Prosperous towns are destroyed and their dwellings are scarcely inhabited afterward, another scene of built abundance becoming an abandoned trace.
terra: Qarun goes out before his people in splendor, establishing the displayed height of wealth that is literally swallowed with his house in 28:81.
terra: Qarun and his house are swallowed into the earth, turning displayed wealth and architectural place into a literal descent below the ground.
terra: Witnesses of Qarun's fall recognize that God expands and constrains provision, joining the swallowed house to the correction of wealth-based honor.
terra: The final home is assigned to those who seek neither elevation nor corruption in the land, exactly reversing 89:11-12 and Pharaoh's علا.

luna: The section’s Pharaoh orders a tower to reach Moses’ God and treats worldly power as lasting. At the close of that narrative, this ayah says everything perishes except God, giving a direct limit to the permanence the tower claims.

luna: The section groups Ad and Thamud through their built works and their end. This ayah mentions both nations and says their dwellings became clear after them, adding the physical remainder to the narrative of their destruction.
terra: The spider's house is the weakest house, supplying the opposite boundary to confidence in columns, rock and monumental shelter.
terra: God expands provision for whom He wills and constrains it, repeating the precise theological correction to “my Lord humiliated me.”
terra: Earlier peoples were stronger, worked the earth and developed it more fully, yet their material achievement did not prevent judgment.
terra: Expansion and constraint of provision are called a sign, warning against reading either condition as a simple verdict on dignity.

luna: The section says human height depends on supports while Allah’s height does not. This ayah repeats the heavens-without-visible-pillars image and pairs it with mountains set in the earth, a direct boundary on human claims to structural mastery. | terra: This second no-pillars formulation joins heaven raised بغير عمد ترونها to mountains cast into earth, bringing both divine supports in the section together.
terra: After identifying what God created, the ayah asks what others have created, drawing a sharp boundary between divine creation and human claims.
terra: Even a mustard seed enclosed inside a rock is brought forth by God, setting divine access against the apparent impenetrability of hard stone.

luna: The section sets human overreach against voluntary humility. This ayah forbids contemptuous turning and walking the earth exultantly, naming the posture that the section’s low, gentle gait reverses. | terra: The command not to walk exultantly on earth opposes monumental self-display with an embodied refusal of height.
terra: Moderating one's gait and lowering one's voice shows the chosen form of descent that follows the prohibition of swagger in 31:18.
terra: The trust is offered to heavens, earth and mountains, which refuse to bear it, making the section's load-bearing image morally explicit.
terra: Iron is softened for David immediately before he is told to measure armor links, setting up the contrast between hard material and fine workmanship.
terra: David is commanded to make full coats of armor and measure their links precisely, a Quranic craft scene close to the section's measuring before cutting.
terra: Solomon's workers make elevated chambers and تماثيل, but the passage commands gratitude, contrasting skilled monumental craft with Aad's boastful use of it.
terra: Solomon's body remains upright only through his staff; when it is eaten he falls, a compact scene of a load-bearing support removed.
terra: The Prophet is told to say that his Lord expands and constrains provision, while most people do not understand the meaning of either condition.
terra: Wealth and children do not bring a person near to God, directly correcting the honor-by-abundance assumption addressed in 34:36 and surah 89.
terra: God expands and constrains provision and replaces what people spend, connecting measured sustenance to responsible use.
terra: Good speech rises to God and righteous action raises it, locating true ascent in word and deed rather than physical height.
terra: God alone holds heaven and earth from passing away; if they cease, no one else can hold them, contrasting divine sustaining with visible supports.
terra: Travelers are asked to see the end of predecessors who were stronger, yet no created strength could frustrate God.
terra: The command to worship God is itself called a straight path, bringing the عبد root and the road image into explicit relation.

luna: The section’s dictionary branch for خ ل ق includes a trace leveled to earth, and it follows towns whose traces disappear. This ayah asks who will revive bones after they have decayed, making erased remains the subject of a resurrection challenge.

luna: The section links the erased trace to the root خ ل ق and the Day of leveling. This answer says the One who created the bones the first time will revive them, completing 36:78 with creation after decay.
terra: A second challenge asks whether the Creator of heavens and earth can create their like, again joining the section's two key words خلق and مثل.

luna: The section connects صَفّ to a flat line and to the ordered gathering. This ayah opens with those arrayed in ranks, a direct example of the same root in an ordered row rather than as a description of earth. | terra: The oath by those ranged صفا echoes the ordered line that the section hears both in angels and in flat ground.
terra: Abraham asks whether his people worship what they carve, carrying the mountain-house verb نحت into the setting of fashioned cult objects.
terra: After the question about human carving in 37:95, Abraham says God created both them and what they make, subordinating craft to creation.

luna: The section reads صفّ as a straight line across a level plain. This ayah says the servants stand in ranks and then glorify God, giving the row a worshipful order rather than the fame-seeking monument. | terra: The angels say “we are indeed the ranged ones,” identifying ordered صف as their own stance.

luna: The section explains Pharaoh’s title as possessor of stakes, driven into earth to hold something in place. This ayah names Pharaoh with that title among earlier rejecters, placing the title in a history of defying messengers. | terra: Pharaoh is again named ذو الأوتاد, confirming that the “owner of stakes” is a recurring Quranic identity rather than a local phrase in surah 89.
terra: Those who avoid worshiping الطاغوت and turn to God receive good news as عباد, placing the section's opposed roots within one ayah.
terra: Lofty chambers built above other chambers are promised by God to the mindful, presenting enduring height as gift rather than a tyrant's self-made claim.
terra: The repeated expansion-and-constraint formula is again made a sign for believers rather than an index of rank.

luna: The section says no human support can preserve a raised monument. This ayah depicts the whole earth in God’s grasp and the heavens rolled up on Resurrection Day, giving the final scale of divine mastery over the built world.
terra: The trumpet makes creatures fall, then a second blast leaves them standing and looking, a bodily version of the section's standing/fallen opposition.
terra: Former peoples were stronger and left greater آثار in the earth, but God seized them, directly answering reliance on monumental traces.

luna: The section’s Pharaoh tries to build a tower to reach upward. This later account has Pharaoh tell Haman to build a tower; the next ayah, 40:37, specifies the hoped-for ascent through the ways of heaven. | terra: Pharaoh again commands Haman to build him a lofty tower, directly repeating the ruler's vertical construction project.

luna: The section links Pharaoh’s tower to his attempt to reach Moses’ God. This neighboring ayah supplies the intended ascent through heavenly ways and Pharaoh’s judgment that Moses is a liar. | terra: The tower sought in 40:36 is meant to reach the routes of the heavens and inspect Moses' God; this ayah supplies the project's arrogant upward aim.
terra: The creation of heavens and earth is greater than the creation of humankind, explicitly rescaling human greatness beneath cosmic creation.
terra: God makes earth a settled place, sky a structure and human forms beautiful, uniting ground, building and measured creation under one maker.
terra: The Quran again points to peoples stronger and more numerous whose acquisitions did not save them, repeating the section's civilizational lesson.
terra: God sets firm mountains above earth and measures its sustenance, bringing stabilizing heights and apportioned provision into the same creation scene.

luna: The section quotes Ad’s claim of unmatched strength. This ayah gives the voice behind construction on high places and works assumed to last, making the monuments an expression of their own confidence. | terra: Aad's boast “who is stronger than us?” is answered inside the ayah by the greater strength of the God who created them.

luna: The section sets Ad’s boast of unmatched power beside works that cannot stand. This neighboring ayah describes a humiliating wind sent after the boast in 41:15, showing that claimed strength did not protect them. | terra: The boast in 41:15 ends in a furious wind and a humiliating punishment, turning self-declared height into abasement.
terra: Thamud receive عذاب الهون after choosing blindness, joining the section's هوان root to the abasement of this very monumental people.

luna: The section says Iram has no likeness among the lands and traces the claim through م ث ل. This ayah uses the same comparison-root to say nothing is like God, setting a finite city’s uniqueness against the ultimate limit on likeness. | terra: “Nothing is like Him” reserves absolute incomparability for God, setting a boundary around the merely relative claim that no city resembled Iram.
terra: God does not expand provision without limit because people would transgress on earth; He sends it by measure, directly linking رزق, measure and طغيان.

luna: The section distinguishes a crushed plain from a path made smooth by passage. This ayah joins the earth as a resting place with roads laid through it, a repeated formulation of the surface-and-route image. | terra: The repeated cradle-and-roads formula again places traversable ways within a divinely prepared earth.

luna: The section portrays Pharaoh’s height and structures as displays of worldly power. Pharaoh here points to Egypt’s kingdom and rivers as proof of his greatness, making the landscape itself part of his boast. | terra: Pharaoh boasts of Egypt's kingdom and rivers flowing beneath him, another self-presentation of earthly possession as superior height.

luna: The section shows Pharaoh’s overreach joined to judging others as low. In the next ayah he calls Moses contemptible and barely articulate; that status judgment contrasts his own claim to height and power.
terra: Pharaoh and his people are drowned after provoking God, completing the descent from his boast in 43:51.
terra: Pharaoh's people are made a precedent and a مثل for later peoples, turning the section's “likeness” word into the exemplary afterlife of a destroyed civilization.
terra: A third Jesus saying identifies worship of God with the straight path, preserving the same root-image relation in another context.
terra: Pharaoh's people leave behind many gardens and springs, beginning a catalog of the settled world abandoned after his fall.

luna: The section describes Pharaoh’s tower, stakes, and claims to supremacy. This ayah lists the fine stations his people left behind, making the loss of their worldly standing concrete. | terra: Crops and noble stations are also left behind, adding cultivated and prestigious places to the ruler's vanished height.
terra: The comforts in which Pharaoh's people delighted are abandoned, completing the reversal from possessed grandeur to empty trace.

luna: The section says Pharaoh’s height and structures could not secure permanence. This neighboring ayah says those possessions were inherited by another people, specifying where the former power went.

luna: The section presents Pharaoh among rulers brought down despite their height. This ayah says the heavens and earth did not grieve for them and they were not reprieved, an explicit image of their departure without lasting claim.
terra: Pharaoh is described as عاليا among the transgressors, putting height and limit-breaking side by side in his own characterization.
terra: Muhammad says he is no unprecedented novelty among messengers; this secondary sense of “without precedent” faintly clarifies what a claim of unmatched newness does and does not mean.
terra: A humiliating punishment answers those who acted arrogantly on earth, making هوان the measured reversal of false elevation.

luna: The section says Ad’s extraordinary built presence does not keep its height. This ayah describes a wind destroying everything by its Lord’s command, leaving only their dwellings visible, a specific aftermath for Ad. | terra: Aad's wind destroys everything by its Lord's command until only their dwellings can be seen, turning an unmatched civilization into nearly erased traces.

luna: The section names a bent back as a secondary contour of the low, settled soul and contrasts voluntary humility with forced lowering. This ayah depicts believers bowing and prostrating, a bodily low posture; the posture link is specific, though the verse uses no root named by the section.
terra: True honor with God belongs to the most mindful, setting an explicit measure of كرامة against wealth, stature and construction.
terra: People are asked to look at the sky God built above them without fissures, contrasting the flawless cosmic structure with vulnerable human monuments.
terra: Earth is extended and firm mountains set in it, another direct formulation of level expanse and anchored elevation.
terra: God destroyed generations stronger in might who ranged through the lands seeking escape, directly answering monumental confidence in power and place.
terra: Aad's destroying wind is introduced as the barren wind sent against them, opening another version of the city's undoing.
terra: The wind of 51:41 leaves whatever it reaches like something decayed, converting apparent solidity into ruined matter.
terra: With 51:44 identifying Thamud, this ayah says they could neither stand up nor help themselves, sharply reversing their stone-cutting strength.
terra: God says He built heaven with power, answering Aad's boast of strength through an incomparably larger construction.
terra: God spreads earth and calls Himself an excellent spreader, providing a creation-side counterpart to eschatological leveling.
terra: Jinn and humans are created to worship God, joining خلق directly to the عبد destination with which the section ends.
terra: The oath by the raised roof most naturally evokes heaven as an elevated canopy, reinforcing the section's divine-building counterimage.
terra: Mountains move away in motion, giving the section's final plain a repeated Quranic setting.
terra: The question whether humans were created from nothing or are themselves creators challenges self-grounded existence beneath every human work.
terra: The next question asks whether they created heavens and earth, scaling the challenge in 52:35 up to cosmic construction.

luna: The section connects Ad’s end with bodies fallen like palm trunks. This neighboring ayah names the violent, continuous wind that leads into the trunk image in 54:20; it supplies the force behind the fall. | terra: A violent, relentless wind is sent against Aad, beginning the action that uproots their column-like bodies in 54:20.

luna: The section reads Ad’s hollow palm trunks as upright forms brought down. This parallel says the wind tore them out like uprooted palm trunks, making the reversal from height to fallen bodies explicit. | terra: The wind uproots people as though they were torn-up palm trunks, another direct reversal from vertical strength to prostrate timber.

luna: The section pairs Thamud’s skill in cutting enormous rock with their destruction. This account says a single cry left them like dry broken stalks, reversing the strength of carved stone into brittle remains. | terra: Thamud are reduced by one blast to dry fragments like a pen-builder's shattered brushwood, hard rock craft ending as brittle debris.

luna: The section’s dictionary branch for خ ل ق includes measuring leather before cutting. This ayah says created things are made according to measure; the link is a secondary root reading, not the verse’s claim about Iram. | terra: “Everything We created by measure” gives the section's craft sense of خلق a concise cosmic formulation.
terra: God raises the sky and sets the balance, joining height to true measure in the same sentence.
terra: The raised sky and balance of 55:7 lead to the command not to transgress in measure, defining طغيان as crossing a set limit.
terra: After raised sky and the ban on transgressing the balance, people are told to establish weight justly and not diminish measure.
luna: The section levels the monuments and dwellings that seemed fixed in the earth. This ayah states that those on earth pass away, extending the leveling image from structures to their makers.
luna: The section leaves human buildings level with the earth. This adjacent ayah says the Lord of majesty and honor remains, completing 55:26’s passing away with what endures.
terra: The coming event is “lowering, raising,” condensing the section's two opposed movements into one description of judgment.
terra: The mountains are pulverized completely, a direct nonlexical parallel to the breaking and leveling denoted by دك.
terra: After their pulverizing in 56:5, the mountains become scattered dust, specifying what remains of former mass and height.

luna: The section says Thamud felt secure in mountain-carved houses. This ayah describes people who thought their fortresses would protect them, yet were expelled from their homes; it gives a direct reversal of confidence in built defense. | terra: A fortified people think their strongholds will protect them, but their houses are destroyed, sharply reversing architectural confidence.

luna: The section calls Ad’s fallen people hollow palm trunks and describes the collapse of raised things. This ayah speaks of palm trees cut down or left standing by God’s permission, a specific reversal between what falls and what remains upright.
terra: A mountain would humble itself and split from fear of God if made to bear the Quran, showing the hardest height lowered and fractured by divine weight.
terra: Creator, originator and fashioner occur together among God's names, distinguishing initiating and forming from the city's claim to novelty.

luna: The section’s monuments stand apart and are later flattened. This ayah praises those who stand in rank in God’s cause like a compact structure, a collective structure whose alignment rather than private height is commended. | terra: Those who stand صفا are likened to a compacted building, uniquely joining the section's row and constructed-body images.
terra: Wealth and children are again named as a test, a repeated boundary on the prosperity judgment made by the human speaker.
terra: God has made a measure for everything, extending the section's crafted proportion beyond buildings and provision into a universal rule.
terra: One whose provision is constrained is told to spend from what God gave, supplying the faithful response to scarcity instead of “my Lord humiliated me.”
terra: Seven layered heavens show no disparity in the Merciful's creation, making faultless proportion the mark of divine workmanship.
terra: God makes the earth ذلولا and commands people to walk its paths, matching the section's walked, smoothed road and contrasting that lived smoothness with violent leveling.
terra: On the Day people are called to prostrate but cannot, showing the boundary between chosen lowering in life and forced incapacity at judgment.
terra: Their eyes are humbled and humiliation covers them because they had refused prostration while able, joining imposed abasement to rejected voluntary descent.

luna: The section names Thamud for carving hard rock and ends with their collapse in their dwellings. This ayah gives their destruction by the overwhelming blast, the force that undoes the apparent security of their stone homes. | terra: Thamud are destroyed by الطاغية, turning the section's root of overstepping into the overwhelming force that brings them down.

luna: The section describes Ad’s people as fallen palm trunks. This neighboring ayah names the furious wind that precedes that image in 69:7, giving the means by which their apparent strength was overturned. | terra: Aad are destroyed by a furious, violent wind; the following ayah supplies the felled-trunk tableau used by the section.

luna: The section says Ad’s tall bodies end as hollow palm trunks lying on the ground. This ayah gives that exact image after the destructive wind, turning the people who boasted of strength into fallen trunks. | terra: Aad lie like hollow palm trunks, so the section's upright column-like bodies appear felled and emptied on the ground.

luna: The section calls attention to a city’s erased trace and to built height brought level with the ground. This neighboring ayah asks whether any remnant of Ad can be seen after the fallen-trunk image in 69:7, supplying the question of what remains. | terra: After the hollow trunks of 69:7, the question whether any remnant remains completes the section's “erased trace” sense.

luna: The section says the root ط غ ي first carries the sense of water exceeding its bounds and also names a high place. This ayah recalls the flood’s water overflowing its limit, directly supplying the physical rise behind that dictionary connection. | terra: When the water طغى it rises beyond its boundary, supplying the physical overflowing sense behind the section's moral account of transgression.

luna: The section describes the earth being struck flat and says mountains lose their separate height. This ayah brings earth and mountains together under one crushing blow, the broad judgment scene behind that image. | terra: Earth and mountains are lifted and crushed دكة واحدة, a direct Quranic counterpart to the repeated leveling in 89:21.
terra: Mountains become like wool, another judgment image of solid height losing both density and shape.
terra: On resurrection people hurry as though toward a نصب; if understood as an erected goal-marker, the simile faintly recalls the section's desert stones set up as signs.

luna: The section contrasts a plain smashed level from a road made smooth by being walked. This ayah describes the earth spread out like a carpet, establishing the surface across which the next ayah’s paths run. | terra: God makes the earth a spread for people, establishing the habitable ground on which the next ayah's broad paths are walked.

luna: The section describes a road made smooth through use. This neighboring ayah says paths are made across the spread earth for people to travel, giving the traveled surface a concrete counterpart. | terra: People travel wide pathways through the spread earth of 71:19, a direct Quranic scene for the section's walked, smoothed road.
terra: Earth and mountains quake and the mountains become a heap of loose sand, replacing stable vertical bodies with collapsing grains.
terra: The mountains are blown away, another concise scene in which the land's dominant heights cease to hold their place.

luna: The section connects the ground leveled by God with mountains described as pegs. This preceding ayah calls the earth a resting place, completing the earth-and-mountain pair that 78:7 supplies. | terra: The earth is made a resting spread immediately before mountains are named as pegs in 78:7, completing the section's paired ground-and-stake image.

luna: The section defines Pharaoh’s stakes as supports driven into the ground. This ayah calls the mountains pegs, giving the same support image to God’s ordering of the earth. | terra: Mountains are made as pegs, setting God's earth-stabilizing أوتادا opposite Pharaoh's claimed stakes.
terra: The mountains called pegs in 78:7 are set moving and become a mirage, giving the surah itself a creation-to-judgment reversal.

luna: The section links the flat plain with the ranks of the final gathering. This ayah says the Spirit and angels stand in a row on that Day, a direct parallel to the ordered heavenly presence. | terra: The Spirit and angels stand صفا on the Day, an especially close parallel to the angels arranged row upon row in 89:22.

luna: The section’s dictionary branch for ط غ ي explains transgression as rising beyond a limit and applies it to Pharaoh. Here Moses is sent to Pharaoh because he has transgressed, the section’s vertical sense stated as a command’s reason. | terra: The command to approach Pharaoh again gives his defining offense as طغى, preparing his later claim to supreme height.
luna: The section cites Pharaoh’s claim to be the highest lord. This preceding ayah says he gathered his people and called out, supplying the public setting for the boast stated in 79:24.

luna: The section reads Pharaoh’s height as overstepping a boundary. Pharaoh’s claim to be the highest lord turns that image into an explicit claim to supreme authority. | terra: Pharaoh declares himself “your highest lord,” converting political height into the ultimate claim of elevation.

luna: The section cites Pharaoh’s claim to be the highest lord. This next ayah says God seized him with punishment in this life and the next, supplying the reversal immediately after the boast in 79:24. | terra: God seizes Pharaoh for exemplary punishment immediately after the claim in 79:24, supplying the forced descent that answers it.
luna: The section turns Pharaoh’s visible height into a warning about overreach. This neighboring ayah says his seizure is a lesson for one who fears, giving the intended response to that example.

luna: The section compares Pharaoh’s tower and Iram’s columns with God’s raising of the heavens without visible supports. This ayah asks whether human creation or the heaven is harder, then names God as its builder. | terra: The challenge “are you harder to create, or heaven?” answers human claims of singular strength with the heaven God built.

luna: The section sets human-built height against God’s own raised heaven. This ayah says its ceiling was raised and proportioned, a divine height that bounds Pharaoh’s attempt to ascend by construction. | terra: God raises heaven's canopy and proportions it, uniting elevated construction with measured fitting.

luna: The section contrasts God’s crushing of the earth with humanly smoothed paths. This ayah says the earth was spread after the heaven was raised, completing the same vertical-and-grounded landscape in creation. | terra: God spreads the earth before 79:32 describes anchoring its mountains, joining prepared ground to fixed height in one creation sequence.

luna: The section contrasts human stakes with supports established by God. In the same creation passage as 79:27–28, this ayah says God set the mountains firmly, repeating the natural peg image in the section. | terra: God anchors the mountains, expressing the fastening action that the section sees in a peg.

luna: The section defines transgression as going above bounds and later contrasts forced lowering with chosen humility. This ayah names the person who transgresses, carrying the same root into the judgment between those two paths. | terra: The person who طغى is singled out, repeating the section's movement from a named tyrant to the general human act of crossing limits.

luna: The section treats raised works as a way of claiming lasting life. This neighboring ayah says the transgressor preferred the nearer life, specifying the worldly preference behind the upward display named in 79:37. | terra: Preferring the nearer life is the concrete orientation paired with transgression in 79:37, explaining what the overreacher raises above the lasting end.
luna: The section shows high structures brought low at judgment. This neighboring ayah names Hell as the transgressor’s destination, giving the consequence of the worldly path in 79:37–38.

luna: The section distinguishes being forcibly brought down from willingly taking a lowly path. This ayah describes the person who fears standing before the Lord and restrains the self from desire, the chosen restraint opposite transgression.

luna: The section’s final image calls a soul into God’s servants and toward the Garden. This neighboring ayah names the Garden as the home of the person who restrains the self in 79:40, completing the chosen path opposite transgression.
terra: The mountains are set in motion, removing the fixity that makes structures and landmarks seem permanent.
terra: God creates, proportions and balances the human being, extending the section's measured-craft sense from leather or city to the body.
terra: God composes the human in whatever form He wills, completing the fitted formation described in 82:7.
terra: The earth is stretched out flat, directly corresponding to the section's leveled eschatological ground.
terra: God creates and proportionally shapes, making formation itself an act of fitting rather than the boast of an unprecedented human city.
terra: Following creation and proportion in 87:2, God determines and guides, completing the section's link between making and measure.
terra: People prefer the nearer life, naming the temporal choice beneath attempts to build or possess as though they would remain.
terra: The hereafter is better and more lasting, supplying the true permanence against the preference stated in 87:16.

luna: The section’s dictionary entry for د ك ك uses a flat-backed, hump-less camel to explain levelness. This ayah asks the reader to consider how the camel was created, a specific animal echo, though it does not mention a missing hump or flat back. | terra: The source dictionary defines دكاء through a camel without a hump; this invitation to contemplate the camel leads directly to raised sky, erected mountains and spread earth.

luna: The section compares human towers with the heaven raised by God without visible columns. This ayah asks its hearer to look at the sky and how it was raised, repeating the vertical image as a sign of divine making. | terra: The sky is presented for contemplation as something raised, echoing the divine elevation that needs no human column.

luna: The section describes mountains as supports and as heights later leveled. This ayah asks how the mountains were set up, placing their established height among signs of the Creator. | terra: The mountains are presented as things set upright, the Quranic verb نصبت closely matching the section's repeated act of erection.

luna: The section’s final scene leaves the earth level after mountains are removed. This ayah asks how the earth was spread out, giving a creation-side counterpart to the judgment plain. | terra: Beside raised sky and erected mountains, the earth is spread out, joining height and level ground within one sequence.

luna: The section names Thamud among those who transgressed and explains ط غ ي as going beyond a limit. This ayah says Thamud denied in their transgression, a direct application of the same moral frame to the rock-carving people.
luna: The section links Thamud’s transgression with overstepping a limit. This next ayah identifies the most wretched one as the one who rose up, specifying the agent within 91:11’s transgression.

luna: The section defines transgression as exceeding a limit and names Thamud among the transgressors. This neighboring ayah records Salih’s warning that the she-camel has her allotted drink, stating the boundary that the next ayah’s people violate.

luna: The section links Thamud’s transgression to their downfall. This next ayah says they denied Salih and hamstrung the she-camel, naming the concrete violation before the punishment summarized in 91:15. | terra: Thamud's end is expressed by God's crushing them and فسواها, giving the rock-carving people a finale of leveling.
terra: A person's wealth does not benefit him when he falls, compressing amassed property, imagined security and downward collapse into one question.
terra: A burden is removed from the Prophet, beginning a small sequence about load, back and elevation that echoes the section's support vocabulary.
terra: The burden had weighed heavily upon the Prophet's back, furnishing a bodily counterpart to a support bending under load.
terra: After the back's burden is removed, the Prophet's remembrance is raised, completing the sequence's movement from weight to elevation.
terra: Humanity is created in the best stature, beginning a two-ayah movement from fitted upright form to the lowest condition.
terra: The well-formed human of 95:4 is returned to the lowest of the low, a direct creation-to-lowering reversal.

luna: The section connects transgression with overstepping and pairs Pharaoh’s rise with human overreach. This ayah uses the named root for the human who transgresses. | terra: The human being transgresses, extending the section's account of elevated peoples into a general diagnosis of human behavior.

luna: The section identifies seeing oneself as beyond need as the condition for human transgression. This neighboring ayah states that cause, linking the image to self-sufficiency that lets a person imagine limits do not apply. | terra: The cause of 96:6 is seeing oneself self-sufficient, the inner claim beneath both monumental strength and Pharaoh's height.
terra: The answer to human transgression in 96:6-7 is to prostrate and draw near, chosen lowering becoming true approach.
terra: Mountains become like carded wool, a vivid transformation of the hardest elevated mass into light, separated fibers.
terra: The person who gathers and repeatedly counts wealth supplies the immediate posture behind the immortality delusion in 104:3.
terra: The wealth-counter supposes his property will make him immortal, stating in personal terms the same delusion carried by Aad's enduring monuments.

luna: The section labels ع م د as a support or pillar carrying a load. This ayah uses the same root for extended columns in the scene of the sealed fire: columns no longer support a monument but belong to confinement. | terra: The عماد root reappears as extended columns enclosing punishment, reversing the column from an emblem of proud support into part of confinement.
terra: No one is comparable to God, again distinguishing divine uniqueness from a created city's unmatched human scale.
